warmup.q: You rebuild your service's JAR with a bug fix, but keep the AOT cache from the previous build. You start it on JDK 25.0.5 with -XX:AOTCache=app.aot. What happens?
options: It runs the fixed code with the full speed-up from the cache
It runs the old code, served from the cache
It warns that the JAR changed, ignores the cache, and runs the fixed code with no archive at all
warmup.why: On 25.0.4 and later the JVM compares the JAR with the cache, warns, and in the default auto mode carries on without the cache, and without the JDK's default archive too, so it starts slower than with no flag. On 25.0.0 to 25.0.3 the check was missing and the old classes really ran (bug JDK-8377932). It refuses to start only if you asked for that with -XX:AOTMode=on. The last section takes it apart.

opening:
Back to the corner shop. Unpacking every box each morning is silly when the stock hardly changes. A sensible shopkeeper leaves yesterday's filled shelves in the back room and wheels them out at opening time. A clever one also keeps a note of which shelves she used and which shortcuts she learned, so tomorrow starts further along.

The JVM can do both. In the last lesson, 793 of a demo's 818 classes said shared objects file: they came ready-made from an archive the JDK ships. You can build a bigger archive that holds your own classes too. On JDK 25 you can build Project Leyden's AOT cache, which keeps the notes as well.

The catch is that each one is easy to switch off by accident, and the JVM says so only in a warning nobody reads. One mistake even makes start-up slower than having no archive at all. In this lesson, we'll look inside the JDK's own archive, add the tracking service's classes to one, train an AOT cache, and then break it on purpose. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a shopkeeper who keeps yesterday's shelves in the back room, and a note of what she used. The JDK's default archive is those shelves, AppCDS adds your own goods, and the AOT cache adds the notes: linked classes, resolved lambdas and, on JDK 25, the profiles. Each one fits only the exact stock it was made from.

Now search the start command and build of one of your services for SharedArchiveFile, AOTCache or Xshare. Then start it once with -Xlog:cds or -Xlog:aot. Did the archive open?

Next, we'll stop starting a JVM at all. What does GraalVM's native image gain by building the whole program ahead of time, and what can it no longer do?

sections.h: The archive every JDK already ships
sections.html:
Start with the cost of an empty back room. Turn the JDK's archive off with -Xshare:off, and java -version alone makes the JVM find, parse and verify 411 classes before it prints a line. With the archive on, it loads 396, and 393 of them come ready-made. Lesson 1's tracking service felt the difference. Over nine runs on JDK 25.0.5, Create VM took 173 ms instead of 62, and the first answer came at 731 ms instead of 529.

That archive is class data sharing, CDS for short: a file of classes the JVM has already parsed and verified, stored in the JVM's own internal form. Every JDK build since JDK 12 ships one, in lib/server/classes.jsa, with about 1,300 core JDK classes. (It came with JEP 341; a JEP, or JDK Enhancement Proposal, is the document that describes a new JDK feature.) In the shop, these are the shelves that came with the shop: the JDK's makers unpacked them before you ever opened.

The file doesn't hold class files. It holds the structures the JVM would otherwise build in metaspace, laid out the way they sit in memory. At start-up the JVM memory-maps the file: it asks the operating system to make the file part of the program's memory. Each page is then read from disk only when it's first touched. The JVM fixes up a few pointers and uses the classes as they are. All of that happens by default; -Xshare:off turns it off, which is mostly useful for lessons like this one.

There's more than one file in that folder, and the JVM picks the one that matches its settings. JDK 25 ships four. classes_nocoops.jsa is for a JVM running without compressed object pointers, the 32-bit object references it uses by default for heaps below 32 GB. The two _coh files are for compact object headers, a smaller layout for the hidden header every object carries. JEP 519 made them a product feature in JDK 25, still off by default.

That tells you what CDS can save and what it can't. It saves finding, parsing and verifying the archived classes: the unpacking and the checking. It doesn't run static initializers. Those still run on first use, in the same order, so lesson 1's 200,000-row table takes just as long with any archive. The research behind this course logged a program's initializer order with and without a JDK 21 archive and a JDK 25 AOT cache, and the output was identical. And an archive does nothing for the JIT, which still starts cold.

An archive saves the unpacking and the checking. Your static initializers and the JIT still run on every start.

Check yourself: with the archive on, java -version loaded 396 classes, and with it off, 411. Why would turning the archive off make the JVM load more classes? (Without the archive, the JVM must generate some classes on the spot that the archive would have supplied ready-made. On JDK 21 the gap is 35: 405 against 440.)

The JDK's shelves arrive ready-made. The tracking service's own classes still come out of boxes, one by one, from file:.

On JDK 21: two files, 405 of 405 shared, 440 with sharing off. The archive saves work, and it also saves the JVM from generating classes on the spot.

sections.h: AppCDS puts your own classes in the archive
sections.html:
The default archive covers the JDK. AppCDS, application class data sharing, adds your own classes to an archive. It has been part of OpenJDK since JDK 10 (JEP 310), and it's the start-up gain you can have on JDK 21 without touching your code. There are three ways to build one.

The dynamic archive (JDK 13 and later, JEP 350) needs one training run: an ordinary run of the program whose extra job is to write down what it loaded. The JVM writes the archive when that run exits:

java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main    # training run
java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main       # every start after

A dynamic archive stores only what the default archive lacks, so it's small: 221,184 bytes for the demo below.

The static archive takes three steps: record the list of classes, dump them into an archive, then use it.

java -Xshare:off -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=app.classlist -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main
java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=app.classlist -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp tracker.jar
java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main

-XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive (JDK 19 and later), used with -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa, folds all this into your normal start command. If the file exists and came from the same JDK, the JVM uses it; if not, it writes one at exit. That's handy on a laptop and wrong for a server that starts from a read-only disk, or one that's thrown away after every run. There, build the archive when you build the program.

ArchiveLadder, in the Try it below, packs a small workload into a JAR and starts it under each setup. On JDK 25.0.5, one run printed:

setup                  loaded  from archive    wall ms
no sharing                909             0        388
default CDS               897           868        187
AppCDS (dynamic)          826           794        153
AOT cache                 959           959         86

Read the counts first, because they don't change from run to run. With AppCDS, the demo's own classes join the JDK's on the ready-made shelves, and the JVM generates fewer classes on the spot. The times come from one run on a busy machine, so treat them as a direction. The research behind this course measured more carefully, with 30 interleaved runs of a 300-class app on JDK 21. AppCDS cut its start-up CPU time about in half, from 349 ms to 171 ms. Leave the last row for the next section.

The archive comes with rules, and the JVM checks them like a strict stock clerk. The class path must hold JAR files, not folders of class files. It must be the same as when the archive was made, or start with it. And if a JAR changed after the archive was made, the JVM refuses the archive. Here's JDK 21 starting a rebuilt JAR with its old archive, trimmed:

[0.020s][warning][cds] hello.jar timestamp has changed.
[0.020s][warning][cds] hello.jar size has changed.
[0.020s][warning][cds,dynamic] Unable to use shared archive. The top archive failed to load: hello.jsa
  version TWO, rebuilt

It warned, ran the new code from the JAR, and kept the default archive for the JDK's own classes. Remember that last detail, because the AOT cache behaves differently.

Build the archive with the program, from the same JARs, and ship the two together.

Check yourself: you add -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa while the class path is a folder of compiled classes. What happens at exit? (JDK 25 refuses with Cannot have non-empty directory in paths. Pack the classes into a JAR first, as ArchiveLadder does.)

AppCDS saves the unpacking. But a class taken from the shelf still has to be linked, every lambda is still built on the spot, and the JIT still learns everything from scratch. That's the work Project Leyden goes after.

code.title: ArchiveLadder.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l02.demo; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.LocalDate; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.function.Predicate; import java.util.jar.JarEntry; import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream; import java.util.regex.Pattern; import java.util.stream.Collectors; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** * Packs this demo package into build/boot02/app.jar, then starts it under each class-sharing * setup: no sharing, the default CDS archive, a dynamic AppCDS archive, and on JDK 25+ the * AOT cache. For each it prints classes loaded, classes from an archive, and the median wall * time of 3 runs. Timings are noisy; the class counts are the part to trust. */ public class ArchiveLadder { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("--work")) { Work.run(); return; } Path classes = Path.of(ArchiveLadder.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation().toURI()); Path dir = classes.getParent().getParent().getParent().resolve("boot02"); // startup/build/boot02 Files.createDirectories(dir); Path jar = packJar(classes, dir.resolve("app.jar")); // CDS wants JARs, not directories List<String> app = List.of("-cp", jar.toString(), ArchiveLadder.class.getName(), "--work"); System.out.printf("JDK %s, app %s%n", Runtime.version(), jar); System.out.printf("%-20s %8s %13s %10s%n", "setup", "loaded", "from archive", "wall ms"); row("no sharing", List.of("-Xshare:off"), app); row("default CDS", List.of(), app); Path jsa = dir.resolve("app.jsa"); // 1. training run: archive written at exit Files.deleteIfExists(jsa); run(List.of("-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=" + jsa), app); row("AppCDS (dynamic)", List.of("-XX:SharedArchiveFile=" + jsa), app); if (Runtime.version().feature() >= 25) { Path aot = dir.resolve("app.aot"); // 2. JEP 514: train and assemble in one command Files.deleteIfExists(aot); run(List.of("-XX:AOTCacheOutput=" + aot), app); row("AOT cache", List.of("-XX:AOTCache=" + aot), app); System.out.printf("archive sizes: app.jsa %,d bytes, app.aot %,d bytes%n", Files.size(jsa), Files.size(aot)); } else { System.out.printf("archive size: app.jsa %,d bytes. Run on JDK 25+ to add the AOT cache row.%n", Files.size(jsa)); } } /** One line of the table: one logged run for the class counts, three quiet runs for the time. */ static void row(String name, List<String> flags, List<String> app) throws Exception { List<String> logged = new ArrayList<>(flags); logged.add("-Xlog:class+load"); List<String> lines = run(logged, app); long loaded = lines.stream().filter(l -> l.contains(" source: ")).count(); long shared = lines.stream().filter(l -> l.endsWith("source: shared objects file")).count(); long[] ms = new long[3]; for (int i = 0; i < ms.length; i++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); run(flags, app); ms[i] = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } java.util.Arrays.sort(ms); System.out.printf("%-20s %8d %13d %10d%n", name, loaded, shared, ms[1]); } /** Runs a child JVM with these flags and returns its output lines. */ static List<String> run(List<String> flags, List<String> app) throws Exception { List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(flags); cmd.addAll(app); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); List<String> out = p.inputReader().lines().toList(); if (p.waitFor() != 0) throw new IllegalStateException("child failed: " + cmd + "\n" + String.join("\n", out)); return out; } /** Puts every class file of this package into a JAR. */ static Path packJar(Path classes, Path jar) throws IOException { Path pkg = classes.resolve("workbench/startup/l02/demo"); try (OutputStream file = Files.newOutputStream(jar); JarOutputStream out = new JarOutputStream(file); Stream<Path> files = Files.list(pkg)) { for (Path f : files.filter(f -> f.toString().endsWith(".class")).sorted().toList()) { out.putNextEntry(new JarEntry(classes.relativize(f).toString().replace('\\', '/'))); out.write(Files.readAllBytes(f)); out.closeEntry(); } } return jar; } /** The "service" being started: a few classes, lambdas, a stream, regex, java.time and formatting. */ static final class Work { record Parcel(String id, long grams, String depot) { } enum Size { LETTERBOX, PARCEL } static void run() { Pattern line = Pattern.compile("(\\w+);(\\d+);([A-Z]{3})"); List<Parcel> parcels = Stream.of("px1;1250;NTH", "px2;990;NTH", "px3;15000;RIV", "px4;20;HIL") .map(line::matcher) .filter(m -> m.matches()) .map(m -> new Parcel(m.group(1), Long.parseLong(m.group(2)), m.group(3))) .toList(); Predicate<Parcel> fitsLetterbox = p -> p.grams() <= 2_000; Map<Size, List<String>> bySize = parcels.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy( p -> fitsLetterbox.test(p) ? Size.LETTERBOX : Size.PARCEL, TreeMap::new, Collectors.mapping(Parcel::id, Collectors.toList()))); String report = String.format("%s %s", LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 2), bySize); if (report.isEmpty()) throw new AssertionError(); } } }

For each it prints classes loaded, classes from an archive, and the * median wall time of 3 runs. Timings are noisy; the class counts are the part to trust. */ private object Anchor private data class Parcel(val id: String, val grams: Long, val depot: String) private enum class Size { LETTERBOX, PARCEL } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "--work") { work() return } val classes = Path.of(Anchor::class.java.protectionDomain.codeSource.location.toURI()) val dir = classes.parent.parent.parent.resolve("boot02") // startup/build/boot02 Files.createDirectories(dir) val jar = packJar(classes, dir.resolve("app-kt.jar")) // CDS wants JARs, not directories val stdlib = Path.of(KotlinVersion::class.java.protectionDomain.codeSource.location.toURI()) val classPath = listOf(jar, stdlib).joinToString(java.io.File.pathSeparator) val app = listOf("-cp", classPath, "workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadderKt", "--work") println("JDK ${Runtime.version()}, app $jar (+ kotlin-stdlib)") println("%-20s %8s %13s %10s".format("setup", "loaded", "from archive", "wall ms")) row("no sharing", listOf("-Xshare:off"), app) row("default CDS", emptyList(), app) val jsa = dir.resolve("app-kt.jsa") // 1. training run: archive written at exit jsa.deleteIfExists() run(listOf("-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=$jsa"), app) row("AppCDS (dynamic)", listOf("-XX:SharedArchiveFile=$jsa"), app) if (Runtime.version().feature() >= 25) { val aot = dir.resolve("app-kt.aot") // 2. JEP 514: train and assemble in one command aot.deleteIfExists() run(listOf("-XX:AOTCacheOutput=$aot"), app) row("AOT cache", listOf("-XX:AOTCache=$aot"), app) println("archive sizes: app-kt.jsa %,d bytes, app-kt.aot %,d bytes".format(jsa.fileSize(), aot.fileSize())) } else { println("archive size: app-kt.jsa %,d bytes. Run on JDK 25+ to add the AOT cache row.".format(jsa.fileSize())) } } /** One line of the table: one logged run for the class counts, three quiet runs for the time. */ private fun row(name: String, flags: List<String>, app: List<String>) { val lines = run(flags + "-Xlog:class+load", app) val loaded = lines.count { " source: " in it } val shared = lines.count { it.endsWith("source: shared objects file") } val ms = List(3) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() run(flags, app) (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 }.sorted() println("%-20s %8d %13d %10d".format(name, loaded, shared, ms[1])) } /** Runs a child JVM with these flags and returns its output lines. */ private fun run(flags: List<String>, app: List<String>): List<String> { val cmd = listOf(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) + flags + app val p = ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start() val out = p.inputReader().readLines() check(p.waitFor() == 0) { "child failed: $cmd\n${out.joinToString("\n")}" } return out } /** Puts every class file of this package into a JAR. */ private fun packJar(classes: Path, jar: Path): Path { JarOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(jar)).use { out -> for (f in classes.resolve("workbench/startup/l02/demo").listDirectoryEntries("*.class").sorted()) { out.putNextEntry(JarEntry(classes.relativize(f).toString().replace('\\', '/'))) out.write(Files.readAllBytes(f)) out.closeEntry() } } return jar } /** The "service" being started: a few classes, lambdas, regex, java.time and formatting. */ private fun work() { val line = Regex("""(\w+);(\d+);([A-Z]{3})""") val parcels = listOf("px1;1250;NTH", "px2;990;NTH", "px3;15000;RIV", "px4;20;HIL") .mapNotNull { line.matchEntire(it)?.destructured } .map { (id, grams, depot) -> Parcel(id, grams.toLong(), depot) } val fitsLetterbox: (Parcel) -> Boolean = { it.grams <= 2_000 } val bySize = parcels .groupBy({ if (fitsLetterbox(it)) Size.LETTERBOX else Size.PARCEL }, { it.id }) .toSortedMap() val report = "%s %s".format(LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 2), bySize) check(report.isNotEmpty()) }

try.expect: On JDK 25.0.5: no sharing 909 loaded, 0 from the archive; default CDS 897 and 868; AppCDS 826 and 794, with a 221,184-byte archive; AOT cache 959 and 959, with an 11,018,240-byte cache. On JDK 21: 855/0, 821/789 and 754/719. The Kotlin twin on JDK 25 gave 875/0, 855/789, 722/656 and 966/966. The counts repeat exactly; the times jumped by a factor of two between runs on a busy machine.

sections.h: Leyden's AOT cache: train, assemble, then run
sections.html:
Project Leyden is the OpenJDK project that moves start-up work out of production runs, the real runs that serve your users. Its first result is the AOT cache, where AOT means ahead of time. It arrived one JEP at a time, and every piece of it is a final, standard feature: no preview flag and no special switch.

JDK What arrived
24 JEP 483: the AOT cache, with classes already loaded and linked; flags -XX:AOTMode, -XX:AOTConfiguration and -XX:AOTCache
25 (LTS) JEP 514: one command, -XX:AOTCacheOutput, to create it. JEP 515: method profiles from training, for faster warm-up
26 JEP 516: the full cache works with every garbage collector, ZGC included
27 no Leyden JEP; -XX:AOTMode=required becomes the name for on
28, in development JEP 544: compiled machine code in the cache

LTS means a long-term-support release, the kind most teams run in production, and JDK 25 is the current one.

The java manual names three phases, and the shop has all three. In training, you run the program on a realistic workload, and the JVM writes what it loaded and linked into an AOT configuration file. That's an ordinary day, with a notebook on the counter. In assembly, the JVM turns that file into the cache, and your program doesn't run: the evening, spent writing up the notes. In production, every start uses the cache. On JDK 25, one command does the first two:

java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main     # training and assembly, JDK 25+
java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main           # production

When training and assembly run at different times, use the two-step form from JDK 24:

java -XX:AOTMode=record -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main
java -XX:AOTMode=create -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp tracker.jar

The one-step command does the same underneath: when the training run ends, it starts a second JVM with -XX:AOTMode=create, as the Try it below shows.

The cache holds more than an AppCDS archive. Normally the JVM links a class lazily. The first time an instruction runs, the JVM turns a symbolic name in the class file, such as java/util/Map.get, into a pointer to the real method. The first run of a lambda costs more. Its invokedynamic instruction, the bytecode that asks a helper method how to make a call, builds the lambda's hidden class on the spot. The AOT cache stores the results of that work from the training run. It holds classes already linked, names and lambda call sites already resolved, and Java objects the JVM would otherwise build at every start, such as its map of modules. On JDK 25 it also stores the method profiles that tell the JIT what's hot.

Look back at the ladder. The AOT cache row loaded 959 classes, more than any other row, and all 959 came from the archive: the JVM loads and links every cached class before main runs. Code the training never ran gets none of this. It loads the usual way, as the lab shows.

The research behind this course measured the gain carefully on JDK 25. For a 300-class app, start-up CPU time fell from 504 ms to 81 ms, wall time from 431 ms to 98 ms, and peak memory from 64 MiB to 42 MiB. A small web service's median time to first request fell from 218 ms to 136 ms. None of that needed a code change.

Train on work that looks like production. The cache only knows the shelves you used.

A cache built from one day's notes fits that day's shop exactly. Change the stock, the supplier or the layout, and it no longer fits.

try.title: Make an AOT cache by hand (JDK 25+)
steps: Run ArchiveLadder once (previous Try it), so startup/build/boot02/app.jar exists. Then cd labs/startup/build/boot02 and use a JDK 25 java.
Run the first command: training and assembly in one go. Find the Launching child process line and the second Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS line, which hands the child its settings.
Run the second command and look for Opened AOT cache.
Predict the count the third command prints. It names a cache file that doesn't exist. Then run it.

code.title: terminal (JDK 25+)
code.html: java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=track.aot -cp app.jar workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadder --work java -XX:AOTCache=track.aot -Xlog:aot -cp app.jar workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadder --work | grep Opened java -XX:AOTCache=nope.aot -Xlog:class+load -cp app.jar workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadder --work | grep -c 'shared objects file'

try.expect: On 25.0.5 the first command printed Temporary AOTConfiguration recorded: track.aot.config, then Launching child process ... to assemble AOT cache track.aot using configuration track.aot.config, a Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: ... -XX:AOTMode=create line, and AOTCache creation is complete: track.aot 11010048 bytes. The second printed [0.020s][info][aot] Opened AOT cache track.aot. The third printed errors ending in Unable to map shared spaces, still ran the program, and counted 0 shared classes: a bad cache path loses the default archive too.

aside.title: Will my framework build the cache for me?
aside.html: Quarkus, a framework for Java services, does from version 3.40. With quarkus.package.jar.aot.enabled=true, it trains the cache while your integration tests run (tests that start the whole program and talk to it from outside) and writes target/quarkus-app/app.aot, which you use with java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -jar quarkus-run.jar. Its aot-jar packaging leaves all class loading to the JDK's own class loaders, the objects that find and define classes, because Leyden doesn't support custom ones yet. The guide repeats the rule from this section: "The more representative your integration tests are of production traffic, the more effective the AOT cache will be." On JDK 21, quarkus.package.jar.aot.type=app-cds builds an AppCDS archive instead.

video.title: Leyden's AOT cache: train, assemble, then start with the classes already loaded and linked

sections.h: A cache fits one JAR, one JDK and one set of flags
sections.html:
The java manual is blunt about it. An AOT cache belongs to one application class path, one JDK release, and one operating system and CPU, and "if any of the above changes, you must recreate the AOT cache". The JVM checks, and in the default auto mode it starts without the cache when a check fails.

A changed JAR is the worst case, because on early JDK 25 builds that check was missing. On 25.0.0 to 25.0.3, and on 26.0.0 to 26.0.1, the JVM never compared the application's JARs with the cache (bug JDK-8377932). Rebuild the JAR, keep the old cache, and the JVM serves the old classes. The research behind this course reproduced it on JDK 25 GA. The log said the class came from shared objects file, and the rebuilt program printed version ONE, the text of the build before. A real shopkeeper would notice last week's stock on her shelves. Those builds didn't.

The fix shipped in JDK 27 and was backported to 25.0.4 and 26.0.2. StaleCacheDemo, in the Try it below, runs the same experiment. On 25.0.5 the JVM rejects the cache and runs the new code (output trimmed):

[0.038s][warning][aot] This file is not the one used while building the AOT cache: 'hello.jar', timestamp has changed, size has changed
[0.038s][error  ][aot] shared class paths mismatch (hint: enable -Xlog:class+path=info to diagnose the failure)
[0.039s][error  ][aot] Unable to map shared spaces
  version TWO, rebuilt

So require JDK 25.0.4 or later (26.0.2 or later on 26), and rebuild the cache with every JAR, in the same build step. On a fixed JDK an old cache can't run old code, but it still costs you the whole gain.

Here's the surprise the opening promised. A cache the JVM can't use leaves you with no archive at all: unlike AppCDS, it doesn't fall back to the default CDS archive. The one-class program in that demo loaded 542 classes from the default archive with no flag, and 0 with the stale cache. Even the version line shows it: java -XX:AOTCache=nope.aot -version ends with mixed mode, where a normal start says mixed mode, sharing. A typo in the file name makes start-up slower than no flag at all.

The garbage collector matters on JDK 25 too. A garbage collector, or GC, is the part of the JVM that frees memory no object uses anymore, and you choose one with a flag. On 25.0.5, a cache trained under the default collector, G1, gave 0 archived classes under -XX:+UseZGC, and all 959 under the Parallel and Serial collectors. JDK 26's JEP 516 removes this limit. Until then, train with the collector you run.

Module and agent options must match as well: --module-path, --add-modules and --enable-native-access should be the same in training and production. The manual also lists "certain JVMTI options" as incompatible. JVMTI is the JVM's tool interface. Agents, add-ons loaded into the JVM to watch or change a program, use it to rewrite classes as they load, so this matters the day someone adds a monitoring agent.

Two flags catch all of this. -Xlog:aot prints Opened AOT cache app.aot. when the cache works, and the reason when it doesn't. -XX:AOTMode=on (JDK 24 to 26; required from JDK 27) makes the JVM stop with Unable to use AOT cache. instead of running without it. Use that in your build's checks, and keep it out of production. The JDK 27 manual warns that your application "may fail to launch" if, for example, a cloud provider's monitoring agent adds an incompatible option.

A cache the JVM can't use is worse than none. Check that it opened, in every build.

Check yourself: you train on JDK 25.0.4 with G1, then deploy the same JAR on 25.0.5 with G1. Does the cache load? (No. The cache records the exact JDK build, and the JVM refuses one made by any other build.)

Even a cache that opens leaves work in every new JVM: the interpreter still runs first, and the JIT still compiles. The next lesson removes the JVM's start-up altogether, at a price.

try.title: Run new code with an old cache
steps: Read StaleCacheDemo. It compiles a one-class program that prints "version ONE", trains a cache on it, rebuilds the JAR to print "version TWO, rebuilt", and starts the new JAR with the old cache.
Run it through Gradle. On JDK 21 it uses a dynamic CDS archive, because there's no AOT cache before JDK 24.

If Gradle runs on JDK 21 and you have a JDK 25, run the class with that JDK's java: java -cp startup/build/classes/java/demo workbench.startup.l02.demo.StaleCacheDemo. Check java -version first, and predict which output you'll get.

code.title: StaleCacheDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l02.demo; import javax.tools.JavaCompiler; import javax.tools.ToolProvider; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.jar.JarEntry; import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream; /** * Builds hello.jar printing "version ONE", trains a cache on it, rebuilds the JAR to print * "version TWO", and runs the new JAR with the old cache. On JDK 25+ the cache is an AOT cache; * on older JDKs it is a dynamic CDS archive. Needs a JDK (it compiles Java source). */ public class StaleCacheDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Path classes = Path.of(StaleCacheDemo.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation().toURI()); Path dir = classes.getParent().getParent().getParent().resolve("boot02-stale"); Files.createDirectories(dir); Path jar = dir.resolve("hello.jar"); boolean aot = Runtime.version().feature() >= 25; Path cache = dir.resolve(aot ? "hello.aot" : "hello.jsa"); Files.deleteIfExists(cache); // 1. build version ONE and train a cache on it build(dir, jar, "version ONE"); run(List.of(aot ? "-XX:AOTCacheOutput=" + cache : "-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=" + cache), jar); // 2. rebuild the JAR, as a new commit would, but keep the old cache build(dir, jar, "version TWO, rebuilt"); // 3. production: new JAR, old cache String flag = aot ? "-XX:AOTCache=" + cache : "-XX:SharedArchiveFile=" + cache; System.out.printf("JDK %s: java %s -cp hello.jar stale.Hello%n", Runtime.version(), flag.replace(dir + "/", "")); for (String line : run(List.of(flag, "-Xlog:class+load"), jar)) { if (line.contains("stale.Hello source:") || line.startsWith("version") || line.contains("[warning]") || line.contains("[error")) { System.out.println(" " + line.replace("file:" + dir + "/", "file:").replace(dir + "/", "")); } } } /** Compiles a one-class program that prints {@code message} and packs it into {@code jar}. */ static void build(Path dir, Path jar, String message) throws Exception { Path src = dir.resolve("src/stale/Hello.java"); Files.createDirectories(src.getParent()); Files.writeString(src, "package stale;\npublic class Hello {\n public static void main(String[] a) {\n" + " System.out.println(\"" + message + "\");\n }\n}\n"); Path out = dir.resolve("classes"); JavaCompiler javac = ToolProvider.getSystemJavaCompiler(); if (javac == null) throw new IllegalStateException("run this on a JDK, not a JRE"); if (javac.run(null, null, null, "-d", out.toString(), src.toString()) != 0) throw new IllegalStateException("javac failed"); Files.deleteIfExists(jar); try (OutputStream file = Files.newOutputStream(jar); JarOutputStream j = new JarOutputStream(file)) { j.putNextEntry(new JarEntry("stale/Hello.class")); j.write(Files.readAllBytes(out.resolve("stale/Hello.class"))); j.closeEntry(); } } static List<String> run(List<String> flags, Path jar) throws Exception { List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(flags); cmd.addAll(List.of("-cp", jar.toString(), "stale.Hello")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); List<String> out = p.inputReader().lines().toList(); p.waitFor(); return out; } }

Compiles a one-class program that prints [message] and packs it into [jar]. */ private fun build(dir: Path, jar: Path, message: String) { val src = dir.resolve("src/stale/Hello.java") j.closeEntry() } } private fun run(flags: List<String>, jar: Path): List<String> { val cmd = listOf(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) + flags + listOf("-cp", try.expect: JDK 21 refuses the archive (hello.jar timestamp has changed, hello.jar size has changed, Unable to use shared archive) and prints version TWO, rebuilt. JDK 25.0.5 prints the timestamp has changed, size has changed warning, Unable to map shared spaces and version TWO, rebuilt, loaded from file:hello.jar. On JDK 25.0.0 to 25.0.3, the research behind this course saw the class come from shared objects file and the program print version ONE instead: the old class, served from the cache.

compare.title: A training entry point in Java and Kotlin

java.title: TrainingMain.java
java.html: /** Starts the service, sends it every kind of request real users send, then exits so the JVM writes the cache. */ public final class TrainingMain { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { TrackingService service = TrackingService.start(); // the same wiring as production for (String request : List.of("track PX-1042", "track PX-2001", "redirect PX-1042", "history PX-2001")) { service.handle(request); // real code paths, test depots } service.stop(); System.exit(0); // JDK 24 and 25 write the training data when the JVM exits } }

kotlin.title: TrainingMain.kt
kotlin.html: /** Starts the service, sends it every kind of request real users send, then exits so the JVM writes the cache. */ fun main() { val service = TrackingService.start() // the same wiring as production listOf("track PX-1042", "track PX-2001", "redirect PX-1042", "history PX-2001") .forEach { service.handle(it) } // real code paths, test depots service.stop() exitProcess(0) // JDK 24 and 25 write the training data when the JVM exits }

compare.note: Both versions do the same three things: start the service exactly as production does, drive every kind of request through it, and exit. The cache doesn't care which language produced the bytecode. What differs is the class path and the entry point. A Kotlin service has kotlin-stdlib as a JAR on its class path, and it must be there, in the same order, in training and in production, or the cache is refused. The Kotlin entry point is the class TrainingMainKt, not TrainingMain. Kotlin 2.x compiles lambdas to invokedynamic, like Java, so the cache can resolve those call sites ahead of time in both languages. Before JDK 26 a training run has to exit to write its data, which is why both versions end the process; JDK 26 adds jcmd <pid> AOT.end_recording for servers that should keep running.

worked.title: Add the AOT cache to your build

steps.say: Pin the JDK, and use the same build of it where you train and where you run. The cache records the exact JDK build and is refused by any other. Pick 25.0.4 or later, so a changed JAR can never run stale classes.
steps.code: # the build machine and the server must print the same line java -version 2>&1 | head -1 # openjdk version "25.0.5" ... must be 25.0.4 or later

steps.say: In the build, put the JAR at the path it will have on the server, then train and assemble in one step. Use the training entry point from the compare block, so the run goes through every kind of request and then exits.
steps.code: cp build/libs/tracker.jar /srv/tracker.jar java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=/srv/app.aot -cp /srv/tracker.jar tracker.TrainingMain # ... AOTCache creation is complete: /srv/app.aot <size> bytes

steps.say: Add a check to the build: start the real entry point with -XX:AOTMode=on and -Xlog:aot, and fail if the cache doesn't open. A wrong path, a different JDK or a changed JAR all make this check fail, loudly, before any user is affected.
steps.code: java -XX:AOTMode=on -XX:AOTCache=/srv/app.aot -Xlog:aot -cp /srv/tracker.jar tracker.SmokeMain \ | grep -q 'Opened AOT cache' || { echo 'AOT cache not used'; exit 1; } # JDK 27+: AOTMode=required

steps.say: Ship tracker.jar and app.aot together, as one unit, and start production without AOTMode. If someone later adds an agent the cache can't work with, the service starts slower instead of not at all.
steps.code: java -XX:AOTCache=/srv/app.aot -cp /srv/tracker.jar tracker.Main

lab.title: Write a recording class loader and a training run
steps: Run the tests once. All ten fail with NotImplementedError.

Implement RecordingClassLoader.loadClass. A class loader is the object that finds a class's bytes and defines the class; this one writes down every class it defines. Outside the prefix, call super.loadClass(name, resolve). Inside it, take getClassLoadingLock(name), return findLoadedClass(name) if the class is already there, otherwise read the class file from parent.getResourceAsStream, call defineClass, and record the name.

Implement defined() and run RecordingClassLoaderTest. Look at the first two tests: Class.forName(name, false, loader) defines one class, and true defines two, because only initialization runs ZoneTable's static initializer, which touches ZoneRules.
Implement TrainingRun.classList (a fresh loader, Class.forName(entryClass, true, loader), getMethod("handle", String::class.java), one invoke per request) and missing (one line of set arithmetic).

Run all the tests until the ten pass. Then read the fixtures in src/test/java/workbench/startup/l02/fixtures/: ParcelDesk is a tiny tracking service, and a training run with tracking requests only never loads Redirect.
hints: Kotlin's synchronized(lock) { ... } is inline, so return c inside it returns from loadClass itself.
parent.getResourceAsStream(path)?.use { it.readBytes() } ?: throw ClassNotFoundException(name) reads the bytes and handles a missing file in one expression.
The tests compare sets of class names, never counts. A count of all loaded classes changes between JDK builds; the classes your own loader defined don't.
lab.done: All ten tests in RecordingClassLoaderTest and TrainingRunTest pass.

drill.title: The commands from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. For tracker.jar with main class tracker.Main, write: (1) the two JDK 21 commands for a dynamic AppCDS archive, (2) the two JDK 25 commands for an AOT cache, (3) the build check that fails if the cache can't be used. Then add a comment saying which JDK 25 update you require, and why.

answer.html: # 1. JDK 21: dynamic AppCDS java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main # 2. JDK 25: AOT cache (training and assembly, then production) java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main # 3. build check only: stop with an error if the cache can't be used (AOTMode=required on JDK 27+) java -XX:AOTMode=on -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -Xlog:aot -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main # Require 25.0.4+ (or 26.0.2+): earlier builds don't check the JAR (JDK-8377932) # and can run stale classes. Rebuild app.aot with every tracker.jar.

recap: CDS maps ready-made classes from a .jsa file. The default archive (JDK 12+) holds about 1,300 JDK classes and is on unless you pass -Xshare:off. It saves loading and verifying, not static initializers or JIT warm-up.

AppCDS adds your classes: a dynamic archive with -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit and -XX:SharedArchiveFile (JDK 13+), a static one with a class list and -Xshare:dump, or -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive (JDK 19+). On JDK 21 it halved a 300-class app's start-up CPU.

The AOT cache is final in JDK 24 (JEP 483), with one-step -XX:AOTCacheOutput and method profiles in JDK 25 (JEPs 514 and 515). It works in three phases, training, assembly and production, and holds linked classes, resolved lambdas, heap objects and profiles, but only for the code the training ran.
Require JDK 25.0.4+ or 26.0.2+ for the AOT cache, and rebuild it with every JAR: earlier builds could run stale classes (JDK-8377932).
A cache the JVM can't use leaves no archive at all, not even the default one. Check it with -Xlog:aot and -XX:AOTMode=on in your build, never in production, and on JDK 25 train with the GC you run.
The limit: even a perfect cache leaves a JVM that interprets first and compiles each hot method again in every new process, so a new copy is still slow for a while.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to keep app.aot from the last build and reuse it, because training adds two minutes to every build. Explain why that's a bad idea, and what happens on JDK 25.0.3 compared with 25.0.5 when the JAR has changed.
explain.answer: The cache belongs to one exact set of JARs, one JDK build and one set of flags. When the JAR changes, the old cache describes classes that no longer exist in that form. On 25.0.3 the JVM didn't check the application's JARs at all, so it would serve the old classes from the cache and run last build's code with no error. On 25.0.5 it notices the changed timestamp and size, warns, and runs without the cache, so the code is right but every start loses the gain, and the JDK's default archive with it. Either way the cache has to be built in the same step as the JAR and shipped with it. Two minutes are cheaper than either failure.

deeper.html:
A few details that matter once you run this for real.

The static archive is dumped in interpreter-only mode, as if -Xint were set, so the output is the same bit for bit every time. For long class lists you can add -Xmixed to speed up the dump when you don't need that.

You can also take an archive from a running process: jcmd <pid> VM.cds dynamic_dump app.jsa, if the process was started with -XX:+RecordDynamicDumpInfo, or jcmd <pid> VM.cds static_dump app.jsa. That suits a service whose real warm-up needs real traffic. To try flags without editing start scripts, JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa works, because the JVM reads that variable at start-up. In AOT cache file names, %p and %t are replaced by the process id and the start time, as in -XX:AOTCacheOutput=tracker%p.aot, so parallel training runs don't overwrite each other.

Old articles sell CDS as a way for many JVMs on one machine to share memory. Count on start-up time instead. Modern JDKs map each archive at a different, random address by default and then patch its pointers, which writes to most of its pages and makes them private to the process. In one JDK 25 process, 11.5 MiB of the 14.4 MiB resident in the AOT cache's mapping were private.

The manual lags behind the code in one place: the JDK 25 page still says the cache holds "Java classes and heap objects" and that profiles will come in a future release, although JEP 515 shipped them in JDK 25.

What's next, as of the JDK 28 development line: JEP 544 moves JIT compilation into the training run and ships the machine code in the cache, while the JIT can still recompile in production, and JEP 545 targets start-up and warm-up with ZGC. Neither is in a released JDK yet, so treat them as previews of where this is going, not as flags to use.
